title: What is the ABA problem in compare-and-swap, why does a plain CAS succeed incorrectly when a value changes from A to B and back to A, and how does AtomicStampedReference fix it?
keyPoints: ABA: a thread reads A, is paused, another thread changes A to B to A, and the first thread's CAS succeeds incorrectly.
Plain CAS checks only the current value, not whether it changed in between.
ABA corrupts lock-free stacks and free-lists where node identity or history matters.
AtomicStampedReference pairs the reference with an int stamp (version number).
CAS succeeds only if both the reference and the stamp match; every update increments the stamp.
AtomicMarkableReference pairs a reference with a boolean mark instead of a full counter.
Java's GC reduces ABA compared to C, but it still occurs with deliberate object recycling or logical round-trips.

s1_definition.oneliner: ABA happens because plain CAS checks only the current value, not whether it changed in between; AtomicStampedReference adds a version stamp so an A-to-B-to-A round trip is caught by the changed stamp.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **ABA problem** – a CAS succeeds incorrectly when a value changes from A to B and back to A while a thread is paused.
- **Root cause** – `compareAndSet(expected, new)` checks only the present value, not its history.
- **Impact** – corrupts lock-free structures (stacks, free-lists) where node identity matters.
- **`AtomicStampedReference`** – pairs a reference with an int stamp; CAS checks both reference and stamp.
- **`AtomicMarkableReference`** – lighter variant with a boolean mark instead of a counter.
- **Java GC** – reduces ABA vs. C, but does not eliminate it with object pooling or logical round-trips.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a shared cash drawer at National Bank of India that should hold one Rs.500 note. Rajesh glances in, sees a Rs.500 note, and gets distracted. Priya takes it out, spends it, and puts a different Rs.500 note back. Rajesh returns, sees Rs.500, and concludes nothing changed. An AtomicStampedReference is a tamper counter on the drawer: every opening ticks the counter, so Rajesh sees the counter advanced even though a Rs.500 note is sitting there again.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  ABA Problem:

  Thread 1         Thread 2              top
  ─────────        ─────────             ─────
  read A                                  [A]
  (paused)         pop A                  [B]
                   pop B                  []
                   push A                 [A]
  CAS(A, C)        ← succeeds (A==A)     [C]
  But A's .next is stale → stack corrupted

  Fix with AtomicStampedReference:

  Thread 1         Thread 2              top (ref, stamp)
  ─────────        ─────────             ──────────────
  read A, stamp=7                        (A, 7)
  (paused)         pop A  stamp→8        (B, 8)
                   pop B  stamp→9        (null, 9)
                   push A stamp→10       (A, 10)
  CAS(A,C,7,8)    ← FAILS (stamp 7 != 10) → retry safely
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The ABA problem is a subtle bug where a plain CAS succeeds incorrectly when a value changes from A to B and back to A. The fix is AtomicStampedReference, which pairs the reference with a version stamp so the round-trip is caught by the changed stamp.

At National Bank of India we hit this in a lock-free free-list of reusable settlement slips. Under stress a slip was handed out twice because a plain CAS missed the round-trip. Switching to AtomicStampedReference eliminated the duplicates.

Remember one sentence: ABA happens because plain CAS checks the value but not its history, and AtomicStampedReference adds a version stamp so an A-to-B-to-A round trip is caught.
